guias.titulo: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy — Classification and severity criteria
guias.fuente: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 222 (2020) · FIGO Guidelines on Preeclampsia Prevention and Management (2019) · ISSHP Classification (2021)
guias.html:
Classification:

  • Chronic: BP ≥140/90 before pregnancy or diagnosed before week 20
  • Gestational: BP ≥140/90 after wk 20, without proteinuria or organ dysfunction
  • Preeclampsia: BP ≥140/90 after wk 20 + proteinuria (≥0.3g/24h) or ≥1 severity criterion, even without proteinuria
  • Chronic with superimposed preeclampsia: worsening + new proteinuria/organ dysfunction
  • Eclampsia: tonic-clonic seizures in preeclampsia, with no other neurological cause

Severity criteria (≥1 confirms severe preeclampsia): BP ≥160/110 on 2 readings 15min apart, thrombocytopenia <100,000, doubled transaminases, creatinine >1.1 or doubled, pulmonary edema, new neuro-visual symptoms.

guias.fuente: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 222 (2020) · FIGO Guidelines on Preeclampsia (2019) · ISSHP 2021
guias.html:
Prophylaxis (high risk): ASA 100-150mg/day PO at night, from wk 12-16 to wk 36. Elemental calcium 1.5-2.0g/day if low intake.

Chronic treatment (BP >140/90): Labetalol 100-400mg PO q8-12h (max 2,400mg/day) · Alpha-methyldopa 250-500mg PO q6-8h · Extended-release nifedipine 20-60mg PO q12-24h.

⚠️ Contraindicated: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, renin inhibitors.

Hypertensive crisis (≥160/110): IV labetalol bolus 20mg → 40mg → 80mg q10min (max 300mg) · IV hydralazine bolus 5-10mg q20min (max 20mg) · Oral nifedipine 10-20mg (not sublingual).

guias.titulo: Magnesium sulfate — Seizure prevention and management
guias.fuente: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 222 (2020) · FIGO 2019 · ISSHP 2021 · MSPyBS Paraguay — National Maternal and Neonatal Code Red Guideline (2nd ed., 2021) · AHA / Universidad de Antioquia / PAHO
guias.html:
Indication: preeclampsia with severity criteria, and eclampsia.

Dose: 4-6g IV loading dose in 100mL 0.9% NS over 15-20 min → continuous maintenance 1-2g/hour IV for 24h postpartum or post-last seizure.

Monitoring: patellar reflex present, RR >12-14/min, urine output >30mL/h.

⚠️ Signs of toxicity: RR<12rpm, absent patellar reflex, oliguria <30mL/h, AV block.

⚠️ Antidote — 10% Calcium Gluconate, two current standards (equivalent in available elemental calcium, not contradictory):

  • National standard (MSPyBS Paraguay, Code Red 2nd ed. 2021): 10% Calcium Gluconate — 1g (10mL) IV slow push over 3 min.
  • Advanced international resuscitation standard (AHA · Universidad de Antioquia · PAHO): 10% Calcium Gluconate — 3g (30mL) IV, or alternatively 10% Calcium Chloride — 1g (10mL) IV.

This is not a dosing error: 1g of calcium gluconate provides ~93mg of elemental calcium, while 1g of calcium chloride provides ~272mg — which is why the international advanced-resuscitation regimen uses a larger volume of gluconate (3g/30mL) to match the elemental calcium delivered by 1g of chloride. Which to use? The national standard for an isolated toxicity sign (RR<12, areflexia, oliguria); the international regimen for frank cardiorespiratory arrest from hypermagnesemia.

guias.titulo: Maternal CPR and perimortem cesarean delivery
guias.fuente: AHA — Circulation 2020;142(suppl 2):S366-S368 · ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 212, Obstet Gynecol 2019;134(4):e132-e140 · Queenan JT, et al. — Management of High-Risk Pregnancy
guias.html:
CPR specifics in pregnancy: continuous manual left uterine displacement (or 15-30° left lateral tilt) from the start, to relieve aortocaval compression; chest compressions slightly higher on the sternum; defibrillation at the same energies as outside pregnancy (not contraindicated).

Fundal height threshold (fundus at or above the umbilicus, ≈20 weeks): from this point on, the gravid uterus causes enough aortocaval compression to invalidate the effectiveness of chest compressions — this is the action threshold, defined by maternal benefit, not fetal viability.

≥22-24 weeks is a separate, later threshold: fetal viability — a secondary consideration about the expected neonatal outcome, not about whether to perform the hysterotomy.

4-5 minute rule: if there is no return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) by 4 minutes of high-quality CPR, begin the cesarean/perimortem hysterotomy incision in situ (do not transfer to the operating room) to achieve delivery by minute 5. The primary goal is maternal: evacuating the uterus improves venous return and compression effectiveness.

Treatment: Ursodeoxycholic acid 10-15mg/kg/day PO + Vitamin K if prolonged.

⚠️ Deliver at any sign of fetal compromise, regardless of pathway or GA.

guias.titulo: Threatened preterm labor (TPL) — Diagnosis and tocolysis
guias.fuente: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 171 (2016, reaffirmed 2020) · NICE NG25 (2019, updated 2022) · FIGO Recommendations on Preterm Birth (2021)
guias.html:
Diagnosis: regular uterine dynamics (≥4/20min) + cervical changes, 22-36+6 wk.

TVUS: CL >30mm rules out TPL · CL <25mm high risk · 20-30mm → biomarkers (fetal fibronectin/PAMG-1).

Tocolysis (22/24-33+6 wk): Nifedipine (1st line) loading dose 10-20mg q20min → maintenance q6-8h · Atosiban (NICE/RCOG) · Indomethacin (before wk 32, do not combine with MgSO4 or nifedipine).

Rescue course: if >14 days have passed, GA <34 wk, imminent risk within 7 days.

guias.titulo: PROM — Latency antibiotic regimens and criteria for delivery
guias.html:
Standard (7 days, 24-34 wk): Days 1-2 IV: Ampicillin 2g q6h + Erythromycin 250mg q6h. Days 3-7 oral: Amoxicillin 500mg q8h + Erythromycin 333mg q8h.

guias.titulo: Fetal structural morphology — 7 systems (20-24 week scan)
guias.fuente: ISUOG Practice Guidelines (2020/2023) — CNS, face, heart · Paladini & Volpe (2018) · Jeanty P et al. 1984 · Mayden KL et al. 1982 · Corteville JE et al. 1991/1992 · FMF/Nicolaides · CDHSG / Jani et al. 2007
guias.html:
Structured system-by-system checklist, 18-24 weeks, immediately after the 2nd-trimester FMF screening.

CNS: cavum septum pellucidum (absent ⚠️), symmetric thalami, cranial shape ("lemon"/"strawberry" sign ⚠️), lateral ventricular atrium (normal <10mm · mild 10-15mm · severe >15mm, measured at the level of the choroid plexus glomus), cisterna magna (normal 3.0-10.0mm; <2-3mm obliterated, >10mm mega cisterna magna), 2T nuchal fold (valid 15.0-20.6 wk, normal <6.0mm), banana sign, and cerebellar vermis agenesis. An obliterated cisterna magna plus a banana sign point toward open spina bifida — correlate with the spine.

Face: orbits, nose, maxilla, palate (retronasal coronal view), and upper lip. Orbital diameters: IOD/OOD ratio >0.40 hypertelorism, <0.25 hypotelorism (rule of thirds).

Spine: bony continuity on longitudinal + axial views, and intact overlying skin.

Chest and heart (+ CDH): situs, 4-chamber view, ventricular/atrial symmetry, interventricular septum (VSD), outflow tracts, 3-vessel and trachea view, aortic arch. Cardiothoracic area ratio: normal 0.25-0.33, cardiomegaly >0.35. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: intrathoracic gastric bubble, side (left Bochdalek ~85%), O/E LHR <25% severe · 25-44.9% moderate · ≥45% favorable.

Abdomen: stomach (rule out "double bubble" — duodenal atresia, ~30% association with T21), abdominal wall/cord (omphalocele vs. gastroschisis), renal pelvic dilation (<33 wk obstructive >10.0mm; ≥33 wk obstructive >10.0mm with a distinct normal cutoff of <7.0mm), kidneys (uni/bilateral agenesis, multicystic dysplasia), single umbilical artery, 2T/3T megacystis (≥16 wk, pathological if longitudinal diameter > [GA in weeks + 12]mm), and "keyhole sign" (PUV).

Limbs: 3 segments per limb (humerus/radius-ulna/hand; femur/tibia-fibula/foot) to avoid missing reduction defects, polydactyly (soft marker for T13/Meckel-Gruber/Bardet-Biedl if isolated), and clubfoot.

Placenta, cord, amniotic fluid, cervix: placental location (low-lying <20mm from the internal os) and cord insertion site (marginal "racquet" vs. velamentous — vasa previa risk, confirm with color Doppler).

guias.html:
Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS: accreta/increta/percreta). Main risk factor: prior cesarean plus anterior placenta previa/low-lying placenta.

⚠️ Golden rule: whenever signs of accreta are present, never attempt manual placental removal — leave the placenta in situ and proceed to en bloc hysterectomy, at a Level III-IV center, with a planned cesarean at 34+0-35+6 weeks.

Risk factors: number of prior cesareans, prior uterine curettage, prior uterine surgery (myomectomy), history of Asherman syndrome — in addition to placenta previa/low-lying placenta and maternal age >35 or IVF, already recorded under Morphology and History.

2D ultrasound signs: loss of the clear zone, myometrial thinning (<1mm), irregular placental lacunae ("Swiss cheese" appearance), interruption of the bladder-uterine interface, placental bulging toward the bladder, focal exophytic mass.

Color Doppler signs: uterovesical and subplacental hypervascularity, bridging vessels, lacunar feeder vessels, parametrial involvement.

FIGO Classification (surgical/histopathological confirmation): Grade 1 (Accreta) · Grade 2 (Increta) · Grade 3a (Percreta limited to the uterine serosa) · Grade 3b (Percreta with urinary bladder invasion) · Grade 3c (Percreta with invasion of other pelvic tissues/organs: broad ligament, vaginal wall, pelvic sidewall or any other pelvic organ, with or without bladder invasion). Jauniaux E, et al. FIGO, Int J Gynecol Obstet 2019;146:20-24.

⚠️ Probability and Extent are calculated using the "CaVeSal Classification" — a proprietary scoring scheme developed by the team (not a published FIGO/ISUOG/ACOG score) that combines risk factors + 2D signs + Doppler signs. The FIGO Classification is a separate data point, based on surgical/histopathological confirmation — it does not replace, and should not be confused with, the CaVeSal Classification.

guias.html:
Modalities: Complete (Manning, 5 variables, 10 points + NST) · Ultrasound-only (8 points, no NST) · Abbreviated (Clark: NST + amniotic fluid) · Vintzileos (graded 0/1/2 plus Grannum placental grade, up to 12 points).

Variables: fetal breathing movements, body/limb movements, fetal tone, NST reactivity, amniotic fluid volume (plus placental grade in Vintzileos).

Management depends on the combination of score × amniotic fluid status × GA, not on the total score alone:

  • 10/10 or 8/10 with normal fluid: expectant management.
  • 8/10 with oligohydramnios: deliver at ≥36-37 wk; if preterm, daily Doppler.
  • 6/10 with normal fluid: reassess in 12-24h (or 2h per MSPyBS), or deliver if at term.
  • 6/10 with oligohydramnios: deliver if viability is assured.
  • 4/10 with normal fluid: if <32 wk, repeat in 2h plus corticosteroids plus MgSO4 plus ductus venosus Doppler; cesarean only if it persists or the Doppler decompensates.
  • 4/10 with decreased fluid: immediate emergency cesarean, regardless of GA.
  • ≤2/10 (any fluid status): immediate emergency cesarean, regardless of GA or fluid.

All markers are acute, except placenta and amniotic fluid, which are chronic markers — key to interpreting a low score in the correct context. If the score indicates delivery and GA is preterm, add lung maturation with corticosteroids.

guias.html:
Baseline FHR: tachycardia >160 bpm · bradycardia <110 bpm (same criterion as the heart rate assessed on the 2T morphology scan — Chest and heart).

Variability: absent, minimal, moderate, or saltatory.

Reactivity: 15×15 rule (≥32 weeks) or 10×10 (<32 weeks).

Decelerations: Dips I/II/III (Caldeyro-Barcia).

Shoulders vs. overshoot — NOT synonyms: shoulders are a reassuring finding (brief acceleration before/after a deceleration, intact autonomic baroreflex); overshoot is a non-reassuring finding (exaggerated/rigid acceleration after a deceleration, associated with evolving hypoxia/acidosis).

⚠️ Special morphological patterns — lambda waves, omega pattern: these are informal visual analogies, frequently used for teaching/clinical purposes, that describe the shape of the tracing, but are not official nomenclature of FIGO, ACOG, or NICHD. The W sign (Welt 1984) is different: it does correspond to a published pattern with its own verified source (biphasic variable deceleration).

guias.titulo: FGR and fetal Doppler — Definitions and diagnostic criteria
guias.fuente: Gordijn SJ, et al. Consensus Delphi (2016) · ISUOG Practice Guidelines (2020) · SMFM Consult Series #52 (2020)
guias.html:
Constitutional SGA: EFW/AC P3-P10, strictly normal Doppler, low risk.

Early FGR (<32 wk): isolated EFW/AC<P3 or UA with absent/reversed flow · or combined (≥2 of: EFW/AC<P10, UA-PI>P95, UtA-PI>P95).

Late FGR (≥32 wk, 70-80% of cases): isolated EFW/AC<P3 · or combined (≥2 of: EFW/AC<P10, drop >2 quartiles, CPR<P5, MCA-PI<P5, UtA-PI>P95).

Late FGR (≥32 wk, 70-80% of cases): isolated EFW/AC<P3 · or combined (≥2 of: EFW/AC<P10, drop >2 quartiles, CPR<P5, MCA-PI<P5, UtA-PI>P95).

guias.html:
Stage I (mild): EFW<P3, or CPR<P5, or UtA-PI>P95, or UA-PI>P95 with present diastolic flow. Doppler every 7 days. Delivery at wk 37.

Stage II (severe): persistent absent end-diastolic flow in UA (AEDF) >50% of cycles. Inpatient monitoring, Doppler every 48-72h. Elective cesarean at wk 34 (after lung maturation course).

Stage III: persistent reversed flow in UA, or DV-PI>P95. Strict hospitalization, Doppler every 24-48h. Cesarean at wk 30 (lung maturation + MgSO4 neuroprotection).

Stage IV: reversed/absent A-wave in DV, umbilical vein pulsations, or STV<3ms. Continuous emergency. Immediate cesarean from wk 26 (or limit of viability).

guias.fuente: MSPyBS Paraguay National Guidelines · SLIPE · Spanish Society of Pediatric Infectious Diseases
guias.html:
High avidity: indicates infection >16 wk before the test, not before conception — calculate GA at testing − 16wk to determine if it could have been in the 1st trimester.

3 levels of prevention: 1️⃣ primary (hygiene) · 2️⃣ secondary (infected mother: Spiramycin 1g q8h, does not cross the placenta) · 3️⃣ tertiary (fetal infection confirmed by amniotic fluid PCR: switch to Pyrimethamine+Sulfadiazine+Folinic acid, which does cross the placenta).

⚠️ Pyrimethamine-Sulfadiazine contraindicated in T1 (teratogenic) and the last month (kernicterus).

Duration: no single consensus — most continue until delivery; variants use alternating 3-week cycles, or others stop 2 weeks before delivery.

guias.titulo: Acute gastroenteritis (AGE) and pregnancy — Etiology, management and antibiotic therapy
guias.fuente: IDSA 2017 · ACOG Committee Opinion No. 614 (2014, reaffirmed 2021) · WHO 2019
guias.html:
Viral etiology (70-80%): Norovirus and Rotavirus (community outbreaks), enteric Adenovirus, Astrovirus. Self-limiting (24-72h): profuse watery diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, low-grade fever.

Bacterial: Campylobacter jejuni (most common bacterial cause), non-typhoidal Salmonella enterica / S. typhi (risk of bacteremia/transplacental spread), Shigella spp. (dysentery, tenesmus, mucus/blood), E. coli (ETEC/EPEC/STEC-EHEC O157:H7), Clostridioides difficile (post-antimicrobial).

Listeria monocytogenes: flu-like illness with fever, myalgias and preceding watery diarrhea. ⚠️ Critical risk: maternal bacteremia with transplacental spread → chorioamnionitis, septic abortion, intrauterine fetal death or severe neonatal sepsis.

Parasitic: Giardia lamblia, Entamoeba histolytica, Cryptosporidium parvum.

General management: hydration and electrolyte rebalancing as the cornerstone. Mild-moderate: ORS in frequent sips. Severe/oral intolerance: admission + 0.9% NS or Lactated Ringer's 2,000-3,000mL/24h, adjusted by electrolyte panel (potassium monitoring).

Safe symptomatic treatment: antiemetics (Doxylamine+Pyridoxine, Metoclopramide 10mg PO/IV q8h, Dimenhydrinate 50mg PO/IV q6-8h) · Acetaminophen 500-1000mg PO q6-8h (max 4g/day). Loperamide restricted use (avoid in inflammatory/dysenteric diarrhea with fever or suspected invasive pathogen, due to risk of toxic megacolon); Racecadotril has limited data in pregnancy.

By trimester:

  • 1st trimester: mandatory differential diagnosis with Hyperemesis Gravidarum (AGE presents with watery diarrhea and sudden onset, unlike HG). Avoid NSAIDs entirely. If antibiotics are required: beta-lactams (Amoxicillin, Ampicillin) or macrolides (Azithromycin), safe during organogenesis.
  • 2nd trimester: dehydration and prostaglandins from the intestinal inflammatory process can irritate the myometrium and trigger uterine activity/threatened late miscarriage. Differential: acute appendicitis (the cecum and appendix rise with the gravid uterus). Monitor FHR and cervical length if regular contractions are present.
  • 3rd trimester: severe bacterial diarrhea and hypovolemia are frequent triggers of preterm labor (PTL) and placental abruption. Electronic fetal monitoring/NST with maternal fever. In the peripartum period, if active bacterial AGE is present (Salmonella, Campylobacter, Listeria): maximize enteric isolation and precautions during delivery (vertical transmission).

Antibiotic therapy — indications: dysenteric diarrhea (blood/mucus + fever ≥38.5°C), suspected/confirmed gestational Listeriosis, suspected invasive Shigella/Campylobacter/Salmonella, immunocompromised pregnant patients, severe dehydration or bacteremia/sepsis.

guias.titulo: Respiratory infections (COVID-19, Influenza and ILI) in pregnancy
guias.html:
ILI (Influenza-Like Illness): sudden-onset fever (≥37.8-38.0°C) + cough or sore throat, with no other diagnosis. Virologic diagnosis: nasopharyngeal swab for multiplex RT-PCR (Influenza A/B, SARS-CoV-2, RSV), or rapid antigen test (high specificity, lower sensitivity — confirm with PCR if clinical suspicion is high and the result is negative).

1st trimester: Acetaminophen 500-1000mg PO q6-8h (max 3-4g/day). Early temperature control is mandatory — sustained hyperthermia >38.5°C during organogenesis is associated with neural tube defects and congenital heart disease. Influenza: Oseltamivir 75mg PO q12h x5d, within the first 48h (safe in all trimesters). Mild COVID-19: hydration and rest, avoid NSAIDs; risk of progression: consider Nirmatrelvir/Ritonavir based on risk-benefit balance.

2nd trimester: continue Acetaminophen and Oseltamivir at standard dosing. Fetal monitoring: FHR and uterine activity (paroxysmal cough and fever can induce myometrial irritability). Moderate/severe COVID-19 requiring O2: Dexamethasone 6mg/day IV/PO x10 days (or until discharge). Hospitalize if SpO2 <94% or tachypnea.

3rd trimester: greater vulnerability — diaphragm elevation reduces functional residual capacity, with risk of rapid hypoxemia and ARDS. Continuous electronic fetal monitoring (NST/CTG). Thromboprophylaxis in hospitalized COVID-19: Enoxaparin 40mg SC/day during admission, extend based on postpartum risk factors. If pregnancy must be ended for maternal respiratory deterioration between wk 24-34: Dexamethasone 6mg q12h (4 doses) — dual purpose (maternal treatment + fetal lung maturation).

Preferred antiviral regimens:

  • Influenza A and B: Oseltamivir 75mg PO q12h x5 days (double to 10 days in immunosuppressed patients or severe ICU cases).
  • High-risk mild-moderate COVID-19: Nirmatrelvir + Ritonavir (Paxlovid) 300/100mg PO q12h x5 days (start within the first 5 days of symptoms).
  • Severe/hospitalized COVID-19 with hypoxemia (SpO2 <94%): Dexamethasone 6mg IV/PO once daily for up to 10 days + Remdesivir 200mg IV day 1, then 100mg IV/day x4 additional days (safe in pregnancy under hepatic/renal monitoring) + weight-adjusted prophylactic Enoxaparin.

guias.html:
The physiologic hypervolemia and baseline tachycardia of pregnancy mask the early signs of shock. The period of greatest risk is the defervescence phase (fever drop, days 3-7), with massive plasma leakage and hemoconcentration.

Obstetric risk: threatened miscarriage, preterm birth, placental abruption, postpartum hemorrhage and vertical transmission (if the illness occurs in the immediate peripartum period).

Group A — no warning signs (supervised outpatient management): acute fever + ≥2 of: myalgias, arthralgias, headache, retro-orbital pain, rash, leukopenia; no decompensated comorbidities and adequate oral tolerance. Abundant oral hydration 2-3L/day. Acetaminophen 500-750mg PO q6h (max 3g/day). ⚠️ Absolute prohibition: NSAIDs, Dipyrone (hypotension/dyscrasias) and Aspirin (hemorrhage/Reye syndrome). Daily clinical review with CBC (Hct/platelets) until 48h post-defervescence.

Group B — every pregnant patient is classified here due to her physiologic vulnerability → requires hospital observation:

  • B1 (no warning signs, with a risk condition): hospitalization for close monitoring and maintenance oral or IV fluid/electrolyte replacement.
  • B2 (with warning signs — incipient leakage): intense/continuous abdominal pain, persistent vomiting (≥3/h or ≥4/6h), fluid accumulation (ascites, pleural effusion, thickened gallbladder wall), mucosal bleeding, lethargy/drowsiness, postural hypotension, hepatomegaly >2cm, rising Hct with rapidly falling platelets. 0.9% NS or Lactated Ringer's 10mL/kg/h x1-2h → if improving: stepwise taper (5-7 → 3-5 → 2-3mL/kg/h) to complete 24-48h; if not improving or Hct rises: manage as Group C.

Group C — severe dengue (hemorrhagic/shock/organ failure, ICU management): dengue shock (weak/undetectable pulse, cold extremities, capillary refill >2sec, pulse pressure ≤20mmHg) or respiratory distress from fluid accumulation; severe hemorrhage (hematemesis, melena, massive genital bleeding/PPH, intra-abdominal bleeding); severe organ involvement (AST/ALT ≥1,000 IU/L, altered consciousness, cardiomyopathy, renal failure).

Resuscitation: crystalloids (Lactated Ringer's or 0.9% NS) 20mL/kg IV bolus over 15-30min. If shock reverses: reduce to 10mL/kg/h x1-2h and taper gradually. If it does NOT reverse after 2-3 boluses: elevated Hct → colloids (Albumin 0.5-1g/kg or synthetic colloids 10-20mL/kg over 30-60min); sharply falling Hct → suspect occult/GI/uterine hemorrhage → immediate packed red blood cell transfusion (10mL/kg).

Platelet transfusion: not recommended prophylactically based on count alone (<20,000-50,000/µL). Indicated for active severe hemorrhage or need for emergency surgery/cesarean with platelets <50,000/µL.

guias.html:
4-5-3 mnemonic rule for the first hour of management of obstetric septic shock (postpartum/endometritis/septic abortion source):

Fluid resuscitation: crystalloids 20-30mL/kg IV bolus within the first hour for hypoperfusion or elevated lactate.

Vasopressor (if MAP<65 despite volume load): Norepinephrine 0.05-0.5mcg/kg/min IV, titrated to MAP≥65.

Empiric antibiotic therapy within the first hour (postpartum/endometritis/septic abortion source): Ampicillin/Sulbactam 3g IV q6h + Gentamicin 5mg/kg/day IV — alternative: Piperacillin/Tazobactam 4.5g IV q6-8h ± Clindamycin (anaerobic/pelvic source coverage).

Obtain blood cultures and achieve source control (uterine evacuation if septic abortion/retained products) without delaying antibiotic initiation.

guias.html:
MRS (11 items): somatic, psychological, urogenital. NAMS/Heinemann scheme (total score only): 0-4 mild · 5-8 moderate · ≥9 severe (consider HRT). SOCHEG scheme (broken down by domain, each with its own severe-alteration cutoff): Somatic (items 1-4) ≥8 · Psychological (items 5-8) ≥6 · Urogenital (items 9-11) ≥3 · Total (items 1-11) ≥15.

HRT by uterine status: no uterus → estrogen alone. Uterus present, perimenopause → sequential/cyclic. Postmenopause → continuous combined.

Transdermal HRT (preferred, especially with hypertension, obesity BMI>30, hypertriglyceridemia, VTE risk): 17β-Estradiol gel 0.75-1.25g/day, or patches 25-50mcg/day.

Endometrial protection (intact uterus): Micronized natural progesterone 200mg/day for 10-14 days/month (sequential regimen) or 100mg/day continuous · or Dydrogesterone 10-20mg/day.

Tibolone (STEAR): 2.5mg/day PO (or 1.25mg/day in lower body weight or advanced perimenopause) — covers vasomotor symptoms, urogenital atrophy and bone loss prevention; does not require an added progestogen.

Tissue-selective estrogen complex (alternative when avoiding a progestogen is preferred): Conjugated equine estrogens 0.45mg/day + Bazedoxifene 20mg/day — bazedoxifene (a SERM) replaces the progestogen for endometrial protection, without the bleeding or breast tenderness associated with it. Evidence from the SMART-1/SMART-2 trials (12 weeks): significant reduction in hot flush frequency/severity vs. placebo, with a 50% reduction by day 8-10 and a sustained ~90% reduction by day 83 of use; no increased risk of breast cancer, endometrial cancer, VTE, stroke or coronary disease in pooled analyses (follow-up up to 2 years — confidence limited by low event incidence and lack of longer-term data). ⚠️ Availability in Paraguay not confirmed — verify locally before prescribing.

Alternative endometrial protection — 52mg LNG-IUD: off-label use alongside systemic estrogen to provide endometrial protection (plus contraception if applicable) — replace at 5 years when used for this purpose (the approved contraceptive lifespan is 8 years, but the evidence supporting endometrial protection in HRT covers up to 5 years).

Local availability (Paraguay, confirm against the current pharmacy/distributor): transdermal 17β-estradiol gel/spray (e.g., Ginoderm) — available. 17β-estradiol vaginal ring — not available. Conjugated equine estrogens + bazedoxifene — availability unconfirmed. This information is contextual, to anticipate the availability conversation with the patient — it should not be used to exclude an option from the clinical list.

Interaction with GLP-1/GIP agonists: the gastric emptying delay induced by semaglutide/tirzepatide (more pronounced with the latter) may reduce absorption of oral HRT — in patients on GLP-1/GIP therapy, prefer the transdermal route for estrogen therapy (same pharmacokinetic principle as in the Contraception during tirzepatide guide).

guias.titulo: Fezolinetant and elinzanetant — NK receptor antagonists, non-hormonal therapy for vasomotor symptoms
guias.fuente: Pratt MC, et al. Expert Rev Clin Pharmacol 2023;16(5):389-398 · Panay N, et al. Climacteric 2024;27(3):221-235 · ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 13. Obstet Gynecol. 2026;148(5):e345-e364 (Table 2)
guias.html:
Mechanism: neurokinin receptor antagonists that act on hypothalamic KNDy neurons involved in thermoregulation, with no hormonal action. Fezolinetant: selective NK3 antagonist. Elinzanetant: dual NK1/NK3 antagonist.

Fezolinetant: 45mg PO once daily, with or without food. FDA-approved for vasomotor symptoms (VMS). ⚠️ FDA boxed warning: requires baseline liver function testing, repeated monthly during the first 3 months of use, and again at 6 and 9 months.

Elinzanetant: 120mg PO once daily. FDA-approved for VMS and also for menopause-related sleep disturbance (a sleep benefit not included in fezolinetant's specific approval). Requires liver function testing before starting and again at 3 months of treatment — a less intensive monitoring cadence than fezolinetant.

Indication (both): moderate-to-severe VMS of the climacteric, a first-line alternative when HRT is contraindicated or not the patient's preference (hormone-dependent cancer history, VTE, personal preference).

In indirect network comparisons (ACOG CPG13), both drugs show similar efficacy on VMS frequency and severity; elinzanetant showed a greater effect on sleep disturbance (PROMIS sleep disturbance score) in indirect comparison with fezolinetant. Most common adverse effects vs. placebo in the OASIS trials with elinzanetant: headache and fatigue.

guias.html:
Interventions with supporting evidence for vasomotor symptoms (VMS), sleep disturbance and mood symptoms of the climacteric — all recommended as adjuncts to hormonal or non-hormonal pharmacologic therapy, not as first-line substitutes when pharmacologic treatment is indicated:

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT): improves VMS, sleep and mood (conditional recommendation, low-to-moderate-quality evidence). Can be delivered in person, by phone, or online.

Mindfulness-based interventions (meditation, body scanning, breathing exercises, yoga): improve sleep and mood (conditional recommendation, low-to-moderate-quality evidence); usual duration 8 weeks in the trials.

Physical exercise: improves sleep and mood (conditional recommendation, low-to-moderate-quality evidence); greatest sleep benefit with 70-90 minute sessions.

Clinical hypnosis: reduces VMS and improves sleep and anxiety symptoms (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence); weekly 45-minute sessions or self-hypnosis programs with a daily 20-minute recording.

Acupuncture: reduces VMS and improves sleep and mood (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence); high heterogeneity across protocols, most trials conducted in China.

⚠️ Natural products and supplements — NOT recommended: the available evidence does not support the efficacy or safety of phytoestrogens (e.g., soy isoflavones) or herbal supplements for the treatment of vasomotor or menopausal symptoms — limited by small sample sizes and heterogeneity of formulations/doses/durations across trials. Since they are not FDA-regulated or evaluated for safety/purity as nutritional supplements, no leading international guideline (ACOG, NAMS/The Menopause Society, IMS) includes them among recommended treatment options.

guias.titulo: Vitamin K2 (MK-7) — Bone and vascular health
guias.fuente: Knapen MHJ, Drummen NE, Smit E, Vermeer C, Theuwissen E. Three-year low-dose menaquinone-7 supplementation helps decrease bone loss in healthy postmenopausal women. Osteoporos Int. 2013;24(9):2499-2507 · Vossen LM, de Leeuw PW, Schurgers LJ, et al. Two Years of Menaquinone-7 Supplementation and Coronary Artery Calcification: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Cardiol. 2026 (online Jun 10, 2026). doi:10.1001/jamacardio.2026.1279
guias.html:
Mechanism: vitamin K2 is a cofactor for the carboxylation of vitamin K-dependent proteins — it activates osteocalcin (calcium binding to bone) and matrix Gla protein/MGP (an inhibitor of soft-tissue calcification, including the arterial wall). Distinct from vitamin K1 (dietary, predominantly hepatic/coagulation-related).

Bone (Knapen et al. 2013, RCT, n=244 healthy postmenopausal women, 3 years): MK-7 180mcg/day decreased age-related loss of bone mineral content (BMC) and bone mineral density (BMD) at the lumbar spine and femoral neck (not at total hip), improved femoral neck bone strength indices, and reduced loss of vertebral height in the lower thoracic region. The source consulted does not publish the exact percentage BMD change figures or p-values — refer to the original article for those numbers before citing them with decimal precision.

Vascular (Vossen et al., VitaK-CAC, JAMA Cardiology 2026, RCT, n=167 with symptomatic coronary artery disease and coronary calcium 50-400 AU, 2 years): MK-7 360mcg/day modestly slowed progression of coronary calcification (Agatston score) vs. placebo (between-group difference p=0.02), with plasma MK-7 levels in the active arm rising from 0.50 to 6.56mcg/L (p<0.001). ⚠️ The authors and the accompanying editorial describe the effect as "modest" and of still-uncertain clinical significance — they call for larger, longer-follow-up trials before considering it an intervention with impact on hard cardiovascular events. No relevant adverse events were reported.

Practical doses (per the evidence cited, two distinct contexts — not interchangeable): bone loss prevention in the climacteric: MK-7 180mcg/day. Cardiovascular context (established coronary disease): the dose studied was 360mcg/day, in a population with already-diagnosed heart disease — there is no equivalent evidence in general primary prevention.

Combination with vitamin D3: both vitamins act on complementary axes of bone metabolism (D3 increases calcium absorption and osteocalcin synthesis; K2 activates/carboxylates it) — see the vitamin D3 dose in the Osteoporosis and bone densitometry guide (above).

guias.titulo: Contraception — General classification and mechanisms of action
guias.fuente: World Health Organization. Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed. 2025 · World Health Organization. Family planning/contraception methods. WHO Fact Sheet, updated 3 July 2025
guias.html:
By family: hormonal (combined estrogen+progestin vs. progestin-only) · barrier (condom, diaphragm, spermicides) · IUD (non-hormonal copper vs. hormonal LNG-IUS) · LARC (implant, IUD/IUS) · permanent (tubal ligation/vasectomy) · fertility awareness-based methods (FABM).

Combined mechanisms (estrogen+progestin): suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis (inhibit the GnRH/FSH-LH surge → anovulation) + thickening of cervical mucus + endometrial thinning.

Progestin-only mechanisms: the dominant and constant effect is thickening of cervical mucus (barrier to sperm migration); suppression of ovulation is dose- and route-dependent — high with the injectable/implant, variable with the minipill.

Copper IUD: local spermicidal/inflammatory effect, non-hormonal (foreign-body reaction + copper cytotoxicity on sperm and the ovum).

LNG-IUS: dominant local endometrial effect (atrophy, mucus thickening) + partial, dose-dependent suppression of ovulation, greater with higher released doses.

Effectiveness of Fertility Awareness-Based Methods for Pregnancy Prevention: A Systematic Review. Obstet Gynecol. 2018;132(3):591-604
guias.html:
Group of non-hormonal methods that identify the fertile window to avoid intercourse (or use a barrier) on those days. Effectiveness is highly dependent on instruction and discipline of use — the gap between perfect use and typical use is the widest of all contraceptive methods (see comparative table).

Calendar/Ogino-Knaus: estimates the fertile window from the history of previous cycles — unreliable with irregular cycles.

Basal body temperature (BBT): detects the post-ovulatory rise (~0.3-0.5°C), retrospectively confirming that ovulation has already occurred — see also the biphasic pattern described in the ovarian cycle physiology guide.

Cervical mucus (Billings method): identifies the elastic/clear mucus around ovulation.

Symptothermal (Sensiplan protocol): combines basal temperature + cervical mucus in a standardized protocol — has shown high effectiveness in studies with intensive training and adherence; those results should not be automatically extrapolated to the whole user population without that same level of instruction.

Standardized mucus methods (Creighton Model FertilityCare System): conceptually derived from Billings, with structured observation and charting; requires formal instruction and follow-up by a certified instructor.

Standard Days Method / CycleBeads: a simplified calendar-based method, included in WHO/CDC recommendations — identifies a fixed fertile window based on cycle day, most useful with regular cycles.

Fertility monitors/apps (e.g. Marquette): algorithms that combine urinary biomarkers (LH, estrogen metabolites) with cervical mucus and/or temperature via a dedicated monitor; evidence of population-level effectiveness is heterogeneous by protocol and device — consider as a support tool, not a substitute for method education.

For FABM effectiveness figures, use the Peragallo Urrutia et al. 2018 systematic review (above) as the main reference — not a single figure for all methods: real-world effectiveness varies a great deal depending on which of these protocols is used and with what level of instruction/adherence, not merely by "being a FABM".

guias.html:
Etonogestrel subdermal implant (Implanon/Nexplanon, 1 rod): approved duration of 5 years — the FDA extended the approval from 3 to 5 years in January 2026, based on a trial (NCT04626596) with no pregnancies and a Pearl Index of 0.0 during years 4 and 5. Dominant mechanism: suppression of ovulation (anovulation) + thickening of cervical mucus. Immediate reversibility upon removal.

2-rod levonorgestrel implant (Jadelle/Norplant-2/Sino-Implant): 5 years. Mechanism somewhat different from etonogestrel: endometrial atrophy and the cervical mucus plug predominate over suppression of ovulation (which is more variable with this implant).

LNG-IUS (levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system) — 3 distinct doses/durations, not a single one:

  • LNG 52mg (Mirena/Liletta/Levosert/Asertia): 8 years.
  • LNG 19.5mg (Kyleena): 5 years.
  • LNG 13.5mg (Jaydess/Skyla — sometimes marketed as a hormonal "Mini IUD", not to be confused with the copper mini-IUD in the following row): 3 years, with lower serum LNG levels and greater preservation of ovulatory cycles than the higher doses.

Copper IUD — duration depends on copper load/frame size, not a single value:

  • High-load (TCu380A and equivalents, e.g. Multiload 375, Nova T, Flexi, T Cu 380A): 10-12 years per WHO (the range depends on the specific product).
  • Reduced-frame/"mini" copper IUD (smaller copper surface area, usually reserved for nulliparous patients or small uterine cavities): shorter duration, typically on the order of 5 years — confirm against the specific model/brand's insert, since a lower copper load corresponds to a shorter approved duration.

Silver-core IUD (Cu-Ag, e.g. Andalan Silverflex): the silver core slows fragmentation/oxidation of the copper wire inside the uterus — a mechanism that in theory extends the device's useful life relative to a pure copper IUD. However, at least one regional manufacturer labels its "Silver T" presentation with a duration of 5 years, shorter than that of high-load copper IUDs — ⚠️ there is real variability between brands/markets; confirm the duration against the specific brand's insert used in your practice before treating it as a single figure for this guide. Regarding silver's "bactericidal" effect: ionic silver does have well-documented general antibacterial activity in the microbiology/materials literature — but the source educational material (AC Hormonal 2025) specifically describes silver's role in the IUD as slowing copper fragmentation, not as a local anti-infective mechanism aimed at reducing PID; ⚠️ I did not find a gynecology-specific source documenting a clinically relevant bactericidal effect of the silver core on pelvic infection risk — if you have a specific reference for that, happy to add it.

All IUDs/IUSs are also useful as post-coital emergency contraception (see following guide).

Non-contraceptive benefits of the LNG-IUS: significantly reduces menstrual bleeding (therapeutic use in AUB, see corresponding guide), and offers some relative protection against symptomatic PID compared with the copper IUD.

Contraindications (MEC Cat 4): see the WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria guide — distortion of the uterine cavity, active pelvic infection, untreated cervical/endometrial cancer (IUDs in general); active breast cancer (LNG-IUS, due to the hormonal component).

guias.titulo: Emergency contraception — Yuzpe, LNG, Ulipristal, Mifepristone, IUD
guias.fuente: World Health Organization. Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed. 2025 · World Health Organization. Selected practice recommendations for contraceptive use, 4th ed. 2025 · World Health Organization. WHO guidelines on expanding contraceptive options, 23 Sept. 2026 (mifepristone as EC — primary text on WHO IRIS blocked to automated access in this session; figures corroborated via independent secondary coverage, DevelopmentAid.org)
guias.html:
LNG, Ulipristal, and Yuzpe share a mechanism: they inhibit or delay ovulation — they are not abortifacients, they do not interrupt an already-implanted pregnancy. Mifepristone (added to this group by WHO in 2026) is the exception on this list: its mechanism is dose/timing-dependent (see detail in its own bullet).

  • Levonorgestrel 1.5mg single dose: effective up to 72-96h, with decreasing effectiveness the more time has passed since intercourse — the sooner, the better.
  • Ulipristal acetate 30mg single dose: effective up to 120h (5 days), and holds its effectiveness better near the day of ovulation than LNG. ⚠️ Reduces the effectiveness of regular hormonal contraception started afterward — use a barrier method or postpone restarting the usual hormonal method by ~5 days.
  • Yuzpe regimen (combined high-dose ethinylestradiol+levonorgestrel, given as 2 doses 12h apart): historical alternative when LNG/Ulipristal are not available — less effective and with more adverse effects (nausea/vomiting) than current dedicated methods.
  • Mifepristone 10-50mg single dose (added by WHO, expanded contraceptive options guideline, Sept. 2026): effective as soon as possible and within 5 days post-coitus. Dose/timing-dependent mechanism: given before the LH surge, it delays/inhibits ovulation just like the other methods in this group; given already in the luteal phase (post-ovulation), its antiprogestogenic effect does demonstrably delay endometrial maturation — unlike LNG (no demonstrated endometrial alteration) and Ulipristal (theoretical antiprogestogen, with no demonstrated anti-implantation effect at the EC dose). Availability and the regulatory framework vary by country — confirm before prescribing. ⚠️ Medico-legal note (relevant given CaVeSal®'s international reach): this mechanistic distinction matters depending on each jurisdiction's legal framework on the onset of life. Where life is considered to begin at fertilization/conception (e.g. Paraguay), a method with no demonstrated anti-implantation effect is not classified as abortifacient; where it is considered to begin at implantation, the distinction loses legal relevance. This guide describes both frameworks without taking a position.
  • Post-coital copper IUD: the most effective method of emergency contraception (failure rate <0.1%), insertable up to 5 days post-coitus — with the added advantage of remaining in place as long-term ongoing contraception.

guias.html:
What it is: a natural estrogen of fetal origin (synthesized by the fetal liver from estriol), with tissue-selective activity — agonist in the CNS, bone and genital tissue, antagonist in breast tissue, and little estrogenic effect in liver and vascular tissue. Hepatic metabolism by glucuronidation only (no CYP450 pathway), which reduces the risk of drug interactions.

Combined formulation: Estetrol 15mg + Drospirenone 3mg, 1 tablet/day.

Efficacy: Pearl Index 1.52 (95% CI 1.04-2.16) in the pivotal phase 3 trials (31 pregnancies / 2,837 women / 26,455 cycles). Regular cycles in 82-94%; spotting ~15% at cycle 12; amenorrhea ~10%.

Coagulation/VTE profile: ⚠️ the available literature does not provide a relative risk or odds ratio for VTE versus other combined hormonal contraceptives — this figure is pending verification against the primary articles before being cited as a number. What is documented: a smaller rise in sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG +54% vs. +74% with ethinylestradiol) and smaller changes in lipid profile, with no change in thrombin generation (Douxfils 2020) — surrogate markers suggesting a smaller hepatic/procoagulant impact than ethinylestradiol, but which do not equate to a confirmed clinical VTE risk figure: the pivotal studies recorded 1 case of DVT in 30,289 cycles, too small a number to estimate a comparative rate. The authors themselves note that these advantages remain mostly theoretical and require post-marketing surveillance.

Why it may be worth raising in consultation: it is an additional option within the combined contraceptive group, useful for an informed conversation with patients who ask about it specifically — the evidence does not yet support positioning it ahead of established combined methods in terms of thrombotic safety.

guias.html:
Semaglutide 0.25→2.4mg/wk. Tirzepatide 2.5→10-15mg/wk. Indication: BMI≥30, or ≥27+comorbidity.

⚠️ "Ozempic babies" (restores ovulation), reduces OCP efficacy, stop ≥2 months preconception, risk of sarcopenia.

Non-response rates (<5% weight loss) by pivotal trial: STEP-1 (semaglutide 2.4mg, non-diabetic adults) 13.6% · STEP-TEENS (semaglutide 2.4mg, adolescents with excess-weight comorbidity) 27% · SURMOUNT-1 (tirzepatide 15mg, non-diabetic adults) 9% · STEP-2 (semaglutide 2.4mg, diabetic adults) 31.2% — response is consistently lower in patients with concomitant type 2 diabetes, a point to anticipate when counseling on expectations.

Maintaining weight loss requires continuing the medication (STEP 4 with semaglutide and SURMOUNT-4 with tirzepatide): in both trials, patients who, on reaching a weight-loss plateau, were randomized to continue the drug maintained or further deepened their weight loss, while those switched to placebo progressively regained weight over the remaining follow-up — obesity behaves here as a chronic condition requiring sustained treatment, not as a short course with a permanent outcome.

GLP-1/GIP + hormone therapy in the climacteric (retrospective cohort, Mayo Clinic): Castaneda et al. (The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology, & Women's Health. 2026;2(2):e118-e128), in 120 postmenopausal women with overweight/obesity on tirzepatide (40 on HRT vs. 80 without, propensity-matched), reported that at 15 months HRT users had 35% greater total body weight loss than non-users, along with additional cardiometabolic improvements in both groups. ⚠️ This is retrospective matched-cohort evidence, not a randomized trial — it suggests a possible synergy but does not establish causality, nor does it by itself change the indication for HRT, which should be decided on its own criteria (see the MRS Scale and HRT guide). Note: the preliminary figure presented at the ENDO 2025 congress (~17% vs. 14%) differs from the final Lancet publication — this guide uses the final published figure (35% relative difference), not the preliminary congress figure.

guias.titulo: EASO 2026 — Algorithm for the pharmacological treatment of obesity and its complications
guias.fuente: Valentinuzzi G, Müller-Wieland D, Holm JC, et al. Framework for the pharmacological treatment of obesity and its complications from the European Association for the Study of Obesity (EASO): 2026 update. Nat Med. 2026
guias.html:
An EASO decision framework that separates two treatment goals depending on whether obesity-associated complications are present — not a single "weight loss" algorithm, but one that guides drug choice by the outcome being targeted:

No complications (mechanical adiposity) — goal: total body weight loss (TBWL): available options (evidence published through Nov 21, 2025, ranked from highest to lowest relative efficacy vs. placebo): tirzepatide, semaglutide, phentermine-topiramate, liraglutide, naltrexone-bupropion, orlistat.

Complications present (metabolic adiposity — deranged endocrine-immune responses) — goal: reverse the affected organ's dysfunction, not just lower weight:

  • OSAS (remission): tirzepatide.
  • Knee osteoarthritis/KOA (pain remission): semaglutide, liraglutide.
  • Prediabetes (normoglycemia restoration): semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide.
  • Type 2 diabetes (remission): tirzepatide, semaglutide, liraglutide, naltrexone-bupropion.
  • Cardiovascular disease (MACE reduction): semaglutide, naltrexone-bupropion.
  • Heart failure (reduced hospitalization): tirzepatide, semaglutide.
  • MASLD/MASH (MASH remission): tirzepatide, semaglutide — new in 2026: liver fibrosis improvement with semaglutide.

The original framework also lists, for each endpoint, the drugs in the same class without available evidence for that specific indication (e.g., orlistat has no MASH remission data) — a drug's absence for a given endpoint does not imply demonstrated inefficacy, only a lack of published evidence as of the framework's cutoff date. Consult the original source for the full drug-by-endpoint detail.

Insulin resistance is a central pathophysiological axis in most patients with PMOS — including many without obesity, according to the Teede et al. 2026 consensus itself that renamed PCOS to PMOS —, not merely an associated comorbidity. Within this, the prevalence of insulin resistance is higher in phenotypes A and B (see the PCOS/PMOS phenotypes guide) than in C/D, per the general PCOS/PMOS phenotype literature (a consistent finding across several case-control studies and meta-analyses, not specific to the Teede paper). This underlies the growing interest in GLP-1/GIP agonists as a metabolic approach in PMOS with an obesity/insulin-resistance component, and in classic insulin sensitizers (metformin, myo-inositol — see next guide) as non-hormonal first-line treatment for ovulatory dysfunction.

Recent supporting evidence: Carmina & Longo (J Clin Med, July 2026) treated 96 women with PMOS and overweight/obesity with semaglutide for 6 months — 52.5% of those previously anovulatory achieved ovulatory cycles, with a response strongly dependent on the degree of obesity (~95% menstrual normalization in overweight vs. ~25% in moderate-severe obesity). The authors propose considering GLP-1 before other fertility interventions in obese patients with PMOS — this is prospective cohort evidence, not a trial that has changed society guidelines.

⚠️ Off-label / evolving use: GLP-1/GIP agonists improve ovulation indirectly (weight loss + improved insulin sensitivity), not through a direct reproductive mechanism. Their formal indication remains the management of obesity/type 2 diabetes — despite the cohort evidence cited above, use specifically directed at PMOS does not yet have endorsement from reproductive society guidelines (ASRM, ESHRE, FLASOG) as a primary indication; approach it as a reasoned extension of its approved metabolic indication, case by case.

guias.html:
Mechanism: myo-inositol and D-chiro-inositol are second messengers in the insulin signaling pathway — supplementation improves ovarian insulin sensitivity, reduces compensatory hyperinsulinemia, and thereby favors resumption of ovulatory cycles in PMOS. It is not a drug in the strict sense but a dietary nutrient/supplement, which shapes its reproductive safety profile (see the inadvertent exposure note below).

Indication: ovulatory dysfunction in PMOS/metabolic phenotype, as an adjunct or alternative to metformin in patients with digestive intolerance to the latter; also used as an adjuvant in ovulation induction/IVF protocols to improve oocyte quality.

Usual dose: Myo-inositol 2-4g/day PO, frequently combined with D-chiro-inositol in the physiological 40:1 ratio (the physiological serum ratio described in healthy ovarian tissue), divided into 1-2 daily doses. Clinical response (resumption of cycles) is expected within 3-6 months of continuous use.

Evidence: the Cochrane review (2023 update) on inositol for PMOS-associated subfertility finds low-to-moderate certainty evidence favoring a possible improvement in clinical pregnancy and ovulation rates versus placebo, with meta-analyses by Unfer et al. and Facchinetti et al. also showing benefit on metabolic parameters (HOMA-IR, androgen profile) — overall evidence quality remains limited by study size and heterogeneity.

Inadvertent exposure during fertility recovery (relevant in women coming off tirzepatide/semaglutide who are improving their metabolic profile): as a physiological nutrient normally present in the diet rather than a synthetic molecule with dedicated teratogenicity studies, myo-inositol is not subject to the same preconception washout restrictions as GLP-1/GIP analogues — no teratogenic warning signal has been described with continued use during an unrecognized pregnancy, and it has in fact also been studied as a supplement for gestational diabetes prevention in at-risk populations. This does not exempt confirming the pregnancy and reassessing the overall therapeutic plan as soon as it is detected.

Specific meta-analysis on myo-inositol and gestational diabetes prevention (Poyatos-León R, et al. Am J Obstet Gynecol. 2026;235(5):1024-1036. DOI 10.1016/j.ajog.2026.05.020): 12 randomized controlled trials, 4,765 women without preexisting diabetes (pregnant or planning conception within 6 months), search through April 2025. Myo-inositol supplementation substantially reduced the risk of gestational diabetes versus control (44% relative risk reduction), with no significant differences in hypertensive disorders, cesarean delivery, macrosomia, preterm birth, or neonatal hypoglycemia.

Phenomenon colloquially described as "Ozempic babies": weight loss and improved insulin sensitivity under GLP-1/GIP treatment can restore spontaneous ovulation in anovulatory women with obesity — sometimes unexpectedly, when the patient assumed she did not need contraception or that the effectiveness of her oral hormonal method was not compromised. ("Ozempic babies" is a descriptive/colloquial term, spread through case reports and medical coverage — it does not correspond to a single formal reference; the underlying clinical basis is the mechanism of ovulatory recovery via weight loss/improved insulin resistance, documented in the international PMOS guideline and in the Carmina & Longo cohort cited in the previous guide.)

Direct clinical implication: every patient on GLP-1/GIP treatment who is not seeking pregnancy should receive active counseling on effective contraception, even if she previously had anovulation due to PMOS — recovery of ovulatory cycles can occur before the patient notices the change (recovery of menstrual regularity), which is why it is important to proactively address both contraception and preconception planning from the start of GLP-1/GIP treatment, not only when it is stopped (see the Contraception during tirzepatide and Preconception washout guides).

guias.html:
Tirzepatide's dual GIP/GLP-1 agonism slows gastric emptying more markedly than pure GLP-1 agonists (semaglutide) — this can reduce the absorption of oral drugs, including oral hormonal contraceptives.

Recommendation: use a non-oral contraceptive method, or add a barrier method, for 4 weeks after starting tirzepatide and after each dose escalation — not only once at treatment start.

⚠️ Do not confuse with preconception washout (next guide): this 4-week window is due to a pharmacokinetic interaction with the oral contraceptive, while preconception washout is the recommended time to stop the drug before trying to conceive — two distinct concepts, with different durations, and both may apply to the same patient at different times.

Practical approach for a patient on tirzepatide who is losing weight and recovering fertility, and who is not seeking pregnancy: prefer non-oral methods whenever possible — LARC (subdermal implant, IUD/IUS — see LARC guide), injectable (DMPA), patch, or vaginal ring — since these do not depend on gastrointestinal absorption and sidestep the underlying problem; if the patient already uses or prefers an oral contraceptive, add a barrier method (condom) for the 4 weeks after starting and after each dose escalation, without needing to stop the oral agent. Discuss contraception from the start of GLP-1/GIP treatment in every woman of reproductive age, not only when she presents seeking pregnancy (see the GLP-1 and fertility recovery guide).

Imbroane et al. (AJOG 2025, observational preconception cohort of 8,534 women) document the underlying clinical context — women recovering ovulatory cycles and fertility during GLP-1/GIP use — that supports the need for this proactive contraceptive conversation, although the study does not directly evaluate contraceptive failure rates.

guias.html:
Semaglutide: the 2026 FDA Wegovy label recommends stopping ≥2 months before trying to conceive, due to its prolonged half-life (~1 week, ~5 half-lives for near-complete elimination).

Tirzepatide: here the regulatory agencies differ, and CaVeSal presents both positions without resolving them, so you can decide according to the patient's context: the European label (EMA/Lilly Mounjaro SmPC) recommends stopping ≥1 month before trying to conceive; the U.S. prescribing information (FDA, Zepbound) does not set a mandatory preconception window and instead instructs discontinuing upon recognizing pregnancy — reflecting a genuine difference in regulatory stance, not an error in either source.

Liraglutide (daily dosing, shorter half-life): common practice uses a shorter washout window (on the order of 1 week), although it is less standardized in the guidelines than semaglutide/tirzepatide.

Dulaglutide, exenatide, lixisenatide: the labels of these older molecules do not set a specific preconception washout window the way semaglutide/tirzepatide do — the usual instruction is to discontinue upon confirming pregnancy, with no preconception interval validated by dedicated studies. ⚠️ Absence of a validated interval does not mean "no need to stop before trying to conceive" — in the absence of specific data, a prudent approach is to apply a criterion similar to semaglutide (weekly-order half-lives) for weekly-depot dulaglutide and exenatide, and one closer to liraglutide for short-acting exenatide/lixisenatide (daily dosing).

Retatrutide: a triple GLP-1/GIP/glucagon agonist still under investigation — not approved for general clinical use as of this guide (see the Incretin development pipeline guide). It therefore has no indication or label for use in a population seeking pregnancy; any exposure would occur in the context of a clinical trial, with its own study-specific contraception/washout protocol — do not extrapolate the windows above to this molecule.

Imbroane et al. (AJOG 2025;233(2):116.e1-e7; n=4,267 per cohort after matching, 8,534 total) found, in their retrospective preconception cohort (TriNetX), an association with lower incidence of gestational diabetes (18.2% vs. 15.2%; OR 0.81; 95% CI 0.72-0.91), hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (22.8% vs. 19.9%; OR 0.84; 95% CI 0.76-0.94), preterm delivery (4.4% vs. 3.0%; OR 0.68; 95% CI 0.54-0.85), and cesarean delivery (19.7% vs. 17.6%; OR 0.89; 95% CI 0.87-0.97) in the group with prior GLP-1/GIP prescription versus the unexposed group. ⚠️ Before matching, the exposed group had a much higher prevalence of overweight/obesity (76.8% vs. 10.7%), type 2 diabetes (37.6% vs. 1.5%), hypertension (32.5% vs. 3.7%), and prior GDM (25.3% vs. 10.0%) — matching adjusted only for age/race/ethnicity/comorbidity categories, not finely for these factors, so much of this apparent protection may reflect residual confounding by indication (who receives GLP-1/GIP) rather than a true protective drug effect. This does not change this guide's preconception washout recommendation — see also the Inadvertent pregnancy during GLP-1/tirzepatide guide for a contrasting read on maternal metabolic/hypertensive outcomes.

Immediate management of an inadvertent pregnancy in a patient using GLP-1/GIP:

  • Stop the drug as soon as pregnancy is confirmed — current evidence does not support continuing it during gestation, regardless of the duration of periconceptional exposure that has already occurred.
  • Reassess the patient's overall metabolic management plan (glycemia, weight, possible metformin indication — see corresponding guide) now in the context of pregnancy, not of weight loss.
  • There is no indication for pregnancy termination based solely on periconceptional GLP-1/GIP exposure — the conversation with the patient should be grounded in the available evidence (summarized below), which so far shows no consistent signal of harm.

What the evidence shows (quick-reference summary, not a substitute for each study's methodological detail):

Brown et al. (Ann Intern Med 2026, target trial emulation, n=3,572) found no significant increase in major congenital malformations associated with periconceptional exposure to GLP-1 agonists, using a design that emulates a randomized trial from observational data to reduce confounding by indication.

D'Antonio et al. (Med 2026, large-scale meta-analysis, n=2,118,215) likewise found no consistent signal of increased risk of adverse obstetric/neonatal outcomes associated with periconceptional or early-pregnancy exposure to GLP-1/GIP agonists — this being the largest sample-size analysis available to date on the topic.

The AJOG 2024 review (PII S0002-9378(24)00864-0) synthesizes the body of evidence available at that time in the same reassuring direction, although — like the rest of this literature — it is based predominantly on observational studies rather than randomized trials specifically designed to assess reproductive safety.

⚠️ All of this evidence is observational (cohorts, target trial emulation, cohort meta-analyses) — absence of a harm signal is not equivalent to definitive evidence of safety, and it does not change the recommendation to stop the drug as soon as pregnancy is recognized, nor the recommendation to respect the preconception washout by molecule when pregnancy is planned (see the Preconception washout by molecule guide).

Malformations — additional meta-analysis (Uysal et al., Sci Rep 2026;16:31416): across 7 cohort studies with over 40,000 exposed pregnancies, there was no significant signal for congenital malformations overall (OR 1.11; 95% CI 0.82-1.51) nor for major malformations with first-trimester exposure (OR 1.39; 95% CI 0.73-2.65). An isolated significant signal was found for urinary malformations (OR 1.24; 95% CI 1.05-1.47), based on unadjusted data from only 2 studies — the authors themselves attribute it most likely to residual confounding (underlying maternal diabetes/obesity), not a direct teratogenic effect. No increased signal was found for stillbirth, spontaneous abortion, small for gestational age, or preterm birth.

Major congenital malformations — largest sample-size meta-analysis available to date (Liu X, et al. Endocrine Connections 2026;15(7). DOI 10.1530/EC-26-0280): across 6 studies (1 prospective + 5 retrospective) with 286,599 women, of whom 43,577 had periconceptional GLP-1RA exposure, there was no significant difference in the risk of major congenital malformations between exposed and unexposed women (RR 1.02; 95% CI 0.96-1.08). No significant signal was found either for preterm birth (RR 1.09; 95% CI 0.80-1.49), large for gestational age (RR 2.31; 95% CI 0.56-9.44), small for gestational age (RR 0.71; 95% CI 0.39-1.27), or stillbirth (RR 1.16; 95% CI 0.24-5.69) — these last three have very wide confidence intervals due to low event numbers, and should be read as "insufficient statistical power to detect a risk if one existed," not as "no risk." The authors themselves note that, given the observational design and limited number of exposed pregnancies, these findings should not be interpreted as proof of safety.

Gestational weight gain and complications after stopping the drug (Maya J, et al. JAMA 2025;334(24):2186-2196 — retrospective cohort, Mass General Brigham, n=448 exposed vs. 1,344 unexposed, matched by propensity score 1:3, 84% with obesity): exposure to GLP-1/GIP between 3 years before and 90 days after conception was associated with greater gestational weight gain (mean 13.7kg vs. 10.5kg; difference +3.3kg; 95% CI 2.3-4.2; p<0.001), a higher risk of excess gestational weight gain (65% vs. 49%; RR 1.32; 95% CI 1.19-1.47), of preterm delivery (17% vs. 13%; RR 1.34; 95% CI 1.06-1.69), of gestational diabetes (20% vs. 15%; RR 1.30; 95% CI 1.01-1.68), and of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (46% vs. 36%; RR 1.29; 95% CI 1.12-1.49) — with no difference in birth length, large/small for gestational age, or cesarean delivery. ⚠️ Unlike Liu et al. (above), which looks for a malformation signal, this cohort looks at the pregnant patient's own metabolic/hypertensive outcomes after periconceptional exposure — a different, and to some extent contrasting, perspective to the reassurance conveyed by Imbroane et al. 2025 (see the Preconception washout by molecule guide): "no malformation signal" does not equal "no maternal risk at all." Cohort composed mostly of women with obesity — limits generalization to a non-obese population.

Gestational weight gain and hypertensive disorders — independent cohort (Pondugula N, et al. Obstet Gynecol. 2026;147(3):293-302. DOI 10.1097/AOG.0000000000005995): a retrospective cohort distinct from Maya et al. (Yale, n=243 exposed up to 1 year before pregnancy — 103 for pregestational diabetes, 140 for weight management — vs. 175 and 200 unexposed, respectively). Found no association between GLP-1RA exposure and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy in either cohort (pregestational diabetes: adjusted OR 0.72; 95% CI 0.42-1.25 · weight management: adjusted OR 0.83; 95% CI 0.45-1.52). There was also no association with gestational weight gain in the pregestational diabetes cohort; in the weight-management cohort, exposure was associated with a lower likelihood of gestational weight gain below recommendations (adjusted OR 0.37; 95% CI 0.18-0.78) — the authors interpret this as a possible rebound weight gain after stopping the drug, not as excess weight gain. ⚠️ Important attribution note: the figures of 65% vs. 49% excess weight gain, 20% vs. 15% gestational diabetes, and 46% vs. 36% hypertensive disorders (above) belong to Maya et al., not to this study — these are two independent cohorts with different findings (Pondugula et al. reports no hypertensive-disorder signal; Maya et al. does).

guias.titulo: Integrated algorithm — GLP-1/GIP and reproductive planning
guias.fuente: Synthesis of the guides in this same section: Contraception during tirzepatide, Preconception washout by molecule, Inadvertent pregnancy during GLP-1/tirzepatide, Metformin in pregnancy, GLP-1 and fertility recovery
guias.html:
Branch 1 — Patient on GLP-1/GIP treatment who is NOT seeking pregnancy (or has not yet decided):

  • Active contraceptive counseling from the start of treatment, even if she previously had anovulation due to PMOS (see the GLP-1 and fertility recovery guide) — fertility can recover before the patient notices.
  • Prefer non-oral methods (LARC, injectable, patch, ring), especially with tirzepatide; if she uses an oral method, add a barrier method for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose escalation (see the Contraception during tirzepatide guide).

Branch 2 — Patient who IS seeking pregnancy (preconception planning):

  • Washout by molecule before attempting to conceive (see the Preconception washout by molecule guide) — different windows for semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide; no validated interval for dulaglutide/exenatide/lixisenatide; retatrutide does not apply, as it is not approved.
  • Reassess baseline metabolic management (metformin, myo-inositol) in a preconception context, not a weight-loss one (see the Metformin in pregnancy and Myo-inositol guides).
  • Preconception folic acid according to risk level (see the Preconception screening and folic acid guide).

Branch 3 — Inadvertent pregnancy already confirmed during GLP-1/GIP use:

  • Stop the drug immediately.
  • Reassess the metabolic plan in a pregnancy context, not a weight-loss one (see the Inadvertent pregnancy during GLP-1/tirzepatide guide).
  • Discuss the available evidence with the patient — reassuring regarding malformations, more mixed regarding gestational weight gain/gestational diabetes/hypertension (see the same guide) — without creating unwarranted alarm or false reassurance.

5 key messages for counseling:

  1. GLP-1/GIP-slowed gastric emptying can reduce absorption of oral contraceptives — discuss it proactively, not reactively.
  2. Fertility recovery from weight loss can occur before the patient notices the menstrual change.
  3. Preconception washout varies by molecule — there is no single rule for "the GLP-1s."
  4. Facing an inadvertent pregnancy, stopping the drug is the immediate step — evidence on malformations is reassuring so far, but evidence on maternal metabolic/hypertensive outcomes is more mixed and warrants active pregnancy follow-up, not just reassurance.
  5. The real teratogen in diabetes is uncontrolled hyperglycemia, not the drug itself — do not stop an antidiabetic agent without an already-defined replacement plan.

guias.html:
The approach to metformin once pregnancy is confirmed depends on why it was prescribed — it is not a single rule:

  • PMOS with ovulation induction/insulin resistance: depending on the clinical context it is continued in early pregnancy or stopped on confirming pregnancy — an individualized, not automatic, decision. Many of these patients reach pregnancy already on metformin and/or myo-inositol as part of their baseline metabolic management (see the PMOS and Myo-inositol guides) — there is no teratogenicity signal for metformin requiring its immediate discontinuation upon confirming pregnancy, unlike GLP-1/GIP analogues (see the Inadvertent pregnancy guide).
  • Prediabetes: individualize according to glycemic control and risk factors. ADA (2026 Standards of Care) does not position metformin as routine in isolated gestational prediabetes — its use follows the same individualization logic as in non-pregnant high-risk patients (elevated BMI, prior GDM, PMOS). NICE (NG3) is somewhat more permissive when risk factors for frank gestational diabetes coexist, where metformin may be anticipated as part of early management if glycemia warrants it — neither guideline indicates it routinely in isolated prediabetes without another risk factor.
  • Pregestational diabetes: ADA prioritizes insulin as first-choice treatment (type 1 and, in most cases, type 2) due to metformin's transplacental passage and a preference for more predictable control; it reserves metformin as an adjunct in type 2 diabetes with high insulin resistance/high requirements, not as monotherapy. NICE (NG3) accepts metformin as first-line or adjunctive therapy in pregestational type 2 diabetes, adding insulin if the glycemic target is not reached — a stance more favorable to oral therapy than ADA's.
  • Gestational diabetes: metformin as a second-line agent versus insulin per ADA (insulin as the preferred first line, metformin as an acceptable alternative after discussing transplacental passage with the patient); NICE (NG3) accepts metformin as a reasonable first line before insulin, barring contraindication or lack of response — see also the algorithm already described in the Gestational Diabetes guide.

Summary of the ADA vs. NICE divergence: both agree that uncontrolled hyperglycemia, not metformin, is the real teratogen, but they differ in how much weight they give oral metformin versus insulin: ADA tends to favor insulin as first-line therapy in overt diabetes (pregestational and gestational), reserving metformin as an adjunct or an alternative discussed case by case; NICE accepts metformin more broadly as a reasonable first line in several scenarios. Neither guideline diverges on PMOS, where the decision is individualized for reasons unrelated to fetal safety.

Key counseling point: the demonstrated teratogen in this context is uncontrolled hyperglycemia — not metformin itself. This should guide the decision not to abruptly stop an antidiabetic agent without an already-defined replacement plan (insulin or another scheme).

Offspring follow-up (MiG TOFU): follow-up of the MiG trial children at 2 years (Diabetes Care 2011) and 7-9 years (BMJ Open Diabetes Res Care 2018) assessed body composition and metabolic outcomes after in-utero metformin exposure — with no signal of harm that would contraindicate its use in gestational diabetes; this is the longest-term support available for this specific indication.

guias.html:
Metformin: compatible with breastfeeding — infant exposure via milk is generally <0.5% of the weight-adjusted maternal dose, with no adverse effects reported (LactMed, updated 15 August 2026; greater caution in newborns, preterm infants, and infants with renal impairment). LactMed also lists a postpartum restart schedule of 500 mg every 12 hours from day one — useful if an immediate postpartum restart is chosen.

Semaglutide: in the only dedicated study to date (Diab et al., Nutrients 2024; 8 women, SC doses 0.25-1 mg/week), semaglutide was not detectable in any of the milk samples analyzed after subcutaneous administration. The authors themselves note the data remain limited — long-term follow-up and data on maternal nutrition/milk composition are lacking. Do not automatically extrapolate this data (subcutaneous semaglutide) to oral formulations.

Tirzepatide: per the Zepbound label (DailyMed, section 8.2), in 11 breastfeeding women after a single 5 mg SC dose, tirzepatide was undetectable in 164 of 171 milk samples; the cumulative amount in the remaining 7 samples represented <0.02% of the administered maternal dose — a reassuring figure, though it comes from a single dose, not continuous use over time.

With this data it is no longer accurate to say "dedicated studies are lacking" for semaglutide/tirzepatide in lactation — they do exist, although small and short-term. Still distinguish the real risk of infant exposure (low, per this preliminary data) from the mere convenience of restarting maternal treatment as soon as possible — two distinct considerations that should not be blended when counseling the patient.

guias.html:
The vitamin D receptor (VDR) is present in multiple tissues of the reproductive tract and neighboring tissues, underlying the clinical associations described in Table 1 of the FLASOG document:

Table 1 — Tissue distribution of the VDR and impact on gyn-obstetric conditions:

  • Ovary and endometrium → PMOS (formerly PCOS), infertility, endometriosis → proposed mechanism: endometrial receptivity, implantation, insulin sensitivity, inflammatory modulation.
  • Placenta → gestational complications (preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, preterm birth) → placental angiogenesis and maternal-fetal immune tolerance.

  • Prevention: 1,000-2,000 IU/day — standard maintenance dose.
  • Insufficiency: 2,000 IU/day or 50,000 IU/month — gradual correction.
  • Moderate deficiency: 50,000 IU every 2 weeks × 6-8 weeks — prioritizes comfort and adherence.

guias.titulo: Vitamin D — Controversy over population screening (FLASOG vs. Neuquén/USPSTF)
guias.fuente: FLASOG — Recomendaciones sobre Vitamina D en Salud Reproductiva (2026) · Comité de Biotecnología, Ministerio de Salud de Neuquén — Boletín Vitamina D (September 2026), citing USPSTF/NICE/CONETEC/Endocrine Society
guias.html:
There is a real, current divergence between organizations over whether population-wide screening (routine 25-OH-D testing) and active supplementation are warranted in healthy women — CaVeSal presents both positions explicitly, without taking sides, so the clinical decision remains in your hands case by case:

FLASOG 2026 position (interventionist): recommends active assessment and supplementation to reach "adequate serum 25(OH)D concentrations" (the document does not set a single numeric target range in its text — see the deficiency/insufficiency thresholds in Table 2 of the previous guide), based on the tissue associations described in the previous guide (preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, preterm birth, PMOS).

Neuquén Bulletin 2026 position (restrictive, citing USPSTF/NICE/CONETEC/Endocrine Society): recommends against routine 25-OH-D testing in the healthy population — available evidence does not consistently demonstrate that screening followed by supplementation improves clinically relevant maternal or fetal outcomes beyond standard population-wide supplementation without prior testing (already in the Supplementation in Pregnancy guide in this same index); reserves targeted testing for specific risk groups.

Both positions come from current literature from different bodies — there is, as of this guide, no single consensus reconciling them. The choice between actively screening or supplementing without prior testing remains at your clinical discretion, case by case.

guias.fuente: MSPyBS Paraguay (2025) · Carel et al. (2009) · Latronico et al. (2016) · Badouraki et al. (2008) · Greulich & Pyle (1959) · Calcaterra et al. (2021) · Kim et al., Korean CPP Guideline (2023) · Nguyen et al., meta-analysis (2021) · Chen et al. (2015) · Eugster (2015)
guias.html:
Definition: onset of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8 (thelarche or adrenarche) or menarche before age 9.

Central precocious puberty (CPP/true, GnRH-dependent): premature activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, with a complete and accelerated isosexual sequence (thelarche → pubarche → menarche). Idiopathic in >80-90% of girls; rule out CNS lesions (hamartomas, gliomas, hydrocephalus), especially if <6 years.

Peripheral precocious puberty (PPP/pseudopuberty, GnRH-independent): autonomous secretion of sex steroids, with basal or suppressed FSH/LH from negative feedback. May be isosexual or contrasexual (virilization).

Non-progressive variants: isolated premature thelarche (no bone-age advance or uterine estrogenization) and idiopathic premature adrenarche (pubic/axillary hair and apocrine odor, with DHEA-S consistent with Tanner II-III and normal basal 17-OHP).

Pelvic ultrasound (transabdominal, with bladder filling) — quantitative criteria:

ParameterPrepubertalPubertal / stimulated
Uterine length<35-40mm≥40-45mm
Uterine volume<2.0-3.0mL≥3.0-4.0mL
Body/cervix ratio1:2 (or 1:1)2:1 (or 3:1)
ConfigurationTubularPear-shaped
Endometrial lineNot visibleVisible/thickened >2mm
Ovarian volume<1.5-2.0mL>2.0-3.0mL
Antral folliclesAbsent or <4mm≥6 of 4-8mm, or dominant >10mm

A pubertal uterus (2:1 ratio, visible endometrium) reflects sustained estrogen exposure — central or ovarian in origin. Strictly prepubertal uterus and ovaries with isolated adrenarche rule out a gonadal origin and point to the adrenal gland.

Anteroposterior and transverse uterine diameters are recorded together with length to calculate volume by the ellipsoid formula (L×AP×T×0.523); they do not carry an independently validated cutoff of their own.

Interpretation and limitations of ultrasound (Calcaterra et al. 2021 · Kim et al., Korean CPP Guideline 2023 · Nguyen et al., meta-analysis 2021 · Chen et al. 2015 · Eugster 2015): pelvic ultrasound is an ancillary/complementary tool, not diagnostic on its own — it is interpreted together with clinical findings, Tanner stage, and hormonal profile. Published cutoffs vary considerably between studies (uterine length ≈32-40mm, ovarian volume ≈1-3mL depending on the series); a meta-analysis of 13 studies found that a uterine length of 3.2cm had a pooled sensitivity of 81.8% and specificity of 82.0% for differentiating precocious puberty from premature thelarche (Nguyen et al. 2021) — useful as a reference point, not as an absolute boundary. After age 8, overlap between prepubertal and early-pubertal values increases considerably (Eugster 2015): in girls aged 8-9, avoid concluding "axis not activated" from ultrasound alone — report in terms of presence or absence of ultrasound signs of estrogenization, and always correlate with Tanner stage and gonadotropins. Follicular distribution (peripheral/diffuse) is documented descriptively: the isolated presence of small follicles does not equal pubertal activation and can be seen normally in prepubertal girls (Eugster 2015).

Algorithm: bone age by left hand-wrist X-ray (Greulich & Pyle) — an advance >1.5-2 years confirms biological impact. Basal LH ≥0.3mIU/mL + elevated estradiol + pubertal uterus → CPP (confirm with GnRH test, LH peak >5mIU/mL, and mandatory brain MRI). Basal LH <0.3mIU/mL (quiescent axis) → evaluate peripheral causes: elevated 17-OHP and DHEA-S → adrenal origin; elevated estradiol with normal 17-OHP → ovarian origin (autonomous follicular cyst, granulosa cell tumor, McCune-Albright).
